summary: This Standards Track document specifies an RTP payload format for MPEG-I haptic data, allowing a haptic unit to be packetized into one RTP packet or fragmented across several. It also updates RFC 9695 regarding the original 'haptics/hmpg' subtype registration.

plainLanguage.summary: Touch and vibration sensations like buzzes get chopped into little packages and sent over the internet.

questions: what is the rtp payload format for haptics
how does haptics fragmentation work in rtp
subtitle: How to carry MPEG-I haptic (touch and vibration) data in RTP packets, and how to describe it in SDP.

tldr.problem: Haptic data is a new kind of media for actuators, alongside audio and video, and the MPEG-I haptic stream had no standard way to travel in RTP packets.
tldr.mechanism: A one-byte RTP payload header marks each MIHS unit as dependent or independent, gives its type and a priority layer. Units go one per packet, fragmented across packets, or aggregated into one packet. New optional SDP parameters describe the stream.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 9695 to add optional parameters to the haptics/hmpg registration and registers the haptics media name for SDP.

facts.label: Payload header size
facts.value: 1 byte (D 1 bit, UT 3 bits, L 4 bits)

today: RFC 9993 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2026 that updates RFC 9695, and the unit metadata shows nothing obsoleting or updating it. It is the RTP payload definition for MPEG-I haptic data as described in the text.

sections.title: Haptics Over RTP
sections.content:
Haptics gives users tactile effects in addition to audio and video. Haptic data mostly goes to devices that act as actuators, which operate according to the values in the haptic effects. The IETF registered haptics as a primary media type, like audio and video, in RFC 9695.

The MPEG Haptics Coding standard (ISO/IEC 23090-31) defines the formats and codec. In it, a haptic stream is made of MIHS units: a unit header plus zero or more MIHS packets. A MIHS unit is the unit of packetization, similar in essence to the NAL unit in some video specifications. This RFC says how to send MIHS units over RTP and defines the SDP parameters and offer/answer rules.

It does not specify synchronization (lip sync) between haptics and audio or video.
sections.plainLanguage: Haptics is the buzzing you feel in a game controller. This RFC is the shipping instruction for sending those buzzes over the internet.

sections.title: The MIHS Stream and Its Units
sections.content:
MIHS has two levels of packetization: units and packets. Four unit types exist:

  • Initialization: metadata needed to reset and initialize a haptic decoder, including a timestamp.
  • Temporal: time-dependent effects such as pressure, velocity and acceleration; the duration is a positive number.
  • Spatial: time-independent effects such as vibrotactile texture, stiffness and friction; the duration is always zero.
  • Silent: no effect during a time interval; the duration is a positive number.

A unit is either independent or dependent. Decoding an independent unit resets previous effects. A dependent unit continues earlier units and cannot be decoded alone. Initialization and spatial units are always independent; temporal and silent units can be either.
sections.plainLanguage: The stream is like a playlist of little clips: a setup clip, a texture clip, buzzing clips and quiet clips. Some clips only make sense after the one before them.

sections.title: RTP Header Use and the Payload Header
sections.content:
The RTP header is the one in RFC 3550, with two fields given special meaning. The marker bit SHOULD be set to one in the first non-silent packet after a period of haptic silence, which helps jitter buffer adaptation and device washout (a reset to a neutral position); in all other packets it MUST be zero. The timestamp is the sampling time of the first sample of the MIHS unit, and its clock frequency MUST equal the sample rate of the haptic data, conveyed out of band such as in SDP.

A one-byte payload header follows the RTP header. Its fields are:

  • D (1 bit): one if the unit is dependent, zero if independent.
  • UT (3 bits): the unit type, from Table 1 of the RFC.
  • L (4 bits): the MIHS layer, a priority order chosen by the sender. Zero is the highest priority, and zero is also used when the sender does not use the field.
sections.plainLanguage: Each parcel has a tiny sticker saying whether it needs earlier parcels, what kind of parcel it is and how important it is.

sections.title: Single, Fragmented and Aggregated Payloads
sections.content:
The UT value identifies the payload structure. Values 1 to 4 are single-unit packets (Initialization, Temporal, Spatial, Silent), 5 is a Single-Time Aggregation Packet, 6 is a Multi-Time Aggregation Packet and 7 is a Fragmentation Unit. Value 0 is unassigned.

Single unit: the RTP header, the payload header and one MIHS unit.

Fragmentation: a large unit is split over several packets, each with the payload header (UT = 7) and an FU header holding FUS (start) and FUE (end) bits, three reserved bits and the unit type. All payload header fields MUST stay unchanged across fragments. Fragments MUST be sent consecutively with ascending sequence numbers and no other packets of the stream in between, and FUs MUST NOT be nested. FUS=1 with FUE=1 is invalid. Missing fragments are typically not retransmitted, so a partly received unit may be dropped or used, depending on the implementation.

Aggregation: an STAP (UT = 5) carries several units with the same timestamp, each preceded by a 16-bit size. An MTAP (UT = 6) carries units with different timestamps, adding a 16-bit timestamp offset per unit equal to the unit's time minus the packet's RTP timestamp. The earliest unit's offset MUST be zero.
sections.plainLanguage: A small thing fits in one envelope. A big thing is cut into numbered pieces with a first and last mark. Several little things sent together can share one envelope.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving MIHS Units
sections.content:
Units can have variable duration, and initialization units declare the duration of later units and its maximum variation. For RTP streaming a sender SHOULD set constant or low-variability durations, so a receiver can tell early (for example with a timer) that a unit was lost.

Silent units signal haptic silence. A sender MAY skip them to save network resources, or send one or a few at the start of a silence. A receiver that gets a silent unit SHOULD assume silence until a non-silent unit arrives, which cuts false loss detections.

In conferences using an RTP video mixer, Full Intra Request (FIR) feedback is recommended. For haptics, the refresh point is an initialization MIHS unit, which resets the decoder to a known state.

On congestion, a receiver or intermediate node MAY prioritize independent units over dependent ones and initialization units over others, and MAY drop silent units first. Nodes SHOULD use the layer value to judge relative importance. Receivers should treat timestamp gaps as loss, validate any CRC16 or CRC32 in units (a unit failing its CRC is treated as lost) and report loss with RTCP Receiver Reports.
sections.plainLanguage: If the road is jammed, throw away the quiet parts first and keep the setup and the important parts. If you do not hear from the sender, it probably means quiet, not lost.

sections.title: SDP Parameters and Negotiation
sections.content:
In SDP, the media name in the m= line MUST be haptics and the encoding name in a=rtpmap MUST be hmpg. The clock rate may be any sampling rate, typically 8000. Optional parameters go in the a=fmtp line as semicolon-separated name=value pairs, without quotation marks.

The parameters are ver (default 2025), profile (simple-parametric or main, default main), lvl (1 or 2, default 2), maxlod, avtypes, modalities, bodypartmask, maxfreq, minfreq, dvctypes and silencesupp (1 to use silence suppression, 0 not to; default 0).

In offer/answer (RFC 3264), ver, profile and lvl MUST match between offer and answer and MUST NOT change later in the session. The other parameters are non-binding recommendations and MAY differ or be updated. In declarative SDP, all parameters describe only the stream, and a receiver that cannot support them MUST reject or not join the session.
sections.plainLanguage: The setup message is a menu card: what kind of buzzing, how detailed, which body parts. Three items must match on both sides. The rest are friendly hints.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Besides the usual RTP payload format threats, haptics has two special risks. Sensors and actuators work in the physical world, so data can leak through sensors or tampering can damage actuators. Misused actuator functions such as force, position, temperature or vibration, or out-of-range keyframe parameters, may harm the user, even when values are permissible for the device. The RFC says transmission should be protected against malicious traffic injection or tampering.

The RFC does not mandate a security mechanism. Applications SHOULD use current strong mechanisms, such as (D)TLS or IPsec. Because the codec uses compression, an attacker may inject pathological datagrams that overload the receiver. End-to-end protection also limits what a Media-Aware Network Element can do, in the case of confidentiality protection even preventing it from discarding packets in a media-aware way.
sections.plainLanguage: Because buzzes happen in the real world, a bad message could hurt someone. So the messages need to be protected from tampering.

sections.title: IANA: Updating haptics/hmpg
sections.content:
The original haptics/hmpg registration in RFC 9695 had no required or optional parameters. This RFC updates it to add the optional parameters, replacing the optional parameters entry and the contact entry, while maintaining backward compatibility. A receiver MUST ignore any parameter not specified in the memo.

It also registers haptics as a media name in the SDP Parameters registry, with the reference RFC 9993.
sections.plainLanguage: The official catalog entry for this haptics format is updated so it can carry the extra settings.

fields.name: D
fields.desc: One if dependent, zero if independent.

fields.name: L
fields.desc: MIHS layer; zero is highest priority.

fields.name: FUS
fields.desc: Set to 1 for the first fragment.

fields.name: FUE
fields.desc: Set to 1 for the last fragment.

fields.name: UT
fields.desc: Type of the unit being fragmented.
